title: What is Critical Thinking? An Introduction
learning_objectives: Define critical thinking in simple, understandable terms.
Recognize why critical thinking is important for university studies and daily life.
Differentiate between everyday thinking and critical thinking.
Identify the core components of critical thinking, such as questioning and analyzing.

scenes.title: Welcome to Critical Thinking!
scenes.narration: Hello everyone, and a very warm welcome to our first week! I'm really excited to begin this journey with you. Today, we're diving into a crucial skill: Critical Thinking. We'll start by simply understanding what it is and why it's so incredibly important, not just for your studies here, but for your everyday life too. Let's get started!
scenes.image_prompt: An educational illustration of a university student looking at a blackboard with 'Critical Thinking' written on it, friendly and inviting.

scenes.title: What is 'Thinking'?
bullet_points: It's how our brain makes sense.
scenes.narration: Before we talk about 'critical thinking', let's just consider 'thinking' itself. Our brains are always working, right? Thinking is what we do automatically to understand the world around us. It's how you decide what to wear in the morning or what to have for dinner. It's our brain's natural way of processing information and making sense of things. But there's a difference between just 'thinking' and 'critical thinking'.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple, friendly illustration of a person's head with abstract thought bubbles floating around it, representing everyday thoughts.

scenes.title: Defining Critical Thinking
scenes.narration: So, what is critical thinking? Think of it as 'thinking about your thinking'. It means you're not just accepting information as it comes. Instead, you're actively and skillfully trying to understand, analyze, and evaluate information. You're thinking clearly and logically, looking for connections between different ideas, and ultimately, using this process to solve problems or make better decisions.
scenes.image_prompt: An educational illustration of a magnifying glass examining a complex thought bubble with interconnected ideas and gears, symbolizing deep analysis.

scenes.title: Why It Matters: University Life
scenes.narration: Why is this skill so important for you, especially here at university? Critical thinking helps you big time with your studies. It allows you to understand complex lecture material, write strong essays that go beyond just summarizing, and meaningfully participate in class discussions. Instead of just memorizing facts, you'll learn how to question them, evaluate arguments, and form your own well-reasoned opinions.
scenes.image_prompt: An illustration of a university student actively taking notes in a lecture hall, with a lightbulb glowing above their head, symbolizing understanding and insight.

scenes.title: Why It Matters: Real-Life
scenes.narration: But critical thinking isn't just for academics. It's a superpower in your everyday life too! Imagine you're seeing a news headline, or someone shares something on social media. Critical thinking helps you ask: 'Is this true? What's the source?' It helps you make smart choices, like deciding which car to buy or who to vote for. It's about being a smart consumer of information and making thoughtful choices.
scenes.image_prompt: An illustration of a person at a crossroads, evaluating different pathways, with a thought bubble showing a balance scale and a question mark, representing decision-making.

scenes.title: Everyday vs. Critical Thinking Example
bullet_points: Everyday: 'The news said it, so it's true.'
Critical: 'Who reported this? What's their evidence?'
scenes.narration: Let's look at a quick example of the difference. Everyday thinking might be hearing a rumor and just accepting it as true, or reading a headline and believing it without question. Critical thinking, on the other hand, means you pause. You ask: 'Where did this rumor come from? Is there any proof? What are the facts behind this headline?' It's about not taking things at face value but digging a little deeper.
scenes.image_prompt: A split screen comparison: on one side, a simple thought bubble; on the other, a more complex thought bubble with interconnected lines, question marks, and a 'verify' icon.

scenes.title: Core Skill: Asking Questions
scenes.narration: So, how do we actually *do* critical thinking? One of the very first steps is to simply ask questions. Don't be afraid to wonder, 'Why is this the way it is?' or 'Is this really true?' Questioning helps you look beyond the obvious. It means challenging your own ideas and the ideas of others. It’s like being a detective, always looking for clues and asking for more information.
scenes.image_prompt: An illustration of a large, bold question mark surrounded by smaller question marks, radiating curiosity and inquiry.

scenes.title: Core Skill: Analyzing Information
scenes.narration: Once you've asked questions, the next step is to analyze the information you have. Analyzing means breaking down a big, complex idea into smaller, more manageable parts. It's like taking a complex machine apart to see how each piece works and how they all fit together. By doing this, you can better understand the whole picture and identify any weak points or important details you might have missed.
scenes.image_prompt: An educational diagram showing a complex concept represented as a jigsaw puzzle, with individual pieces being pulled apart and labeled for analysis.

scenes.title: Core Skill: Evaluating Ideas
scenes.narration: After analyzing, you move on to evaluating. This is where you judge the quality and strength of the information or ideas you're looking at. You'll ask: 'Is the evidence strong enough to support this claim?' 'Is the source of this information reliable?' It's about weighing different arguments, looking for bias, and deciding what makes the most sense based on the facts you have. This helps you form a solid conclusion.
scenes.image_prompt: An illustration of a classic balance scale, with different ideas or pieces of evidence placed on each pan, representing the act of evaluation and weighing options.

scenes.title: Putting It All Together: A Simple Example
bullet_points: Question: 'Which phone is best for me?'
Evaluate: Weigh pros and cons based on your needs.
scenes.narration: Let's quickly put these steps together with a simple example: choosing a new smartphone. First, you'd *question*: 'What do I need in a phone?' Then, you'd *analyze*: you'd compare different models, look at their features, prices, and read reviews. Finally, you'd *evaluate*: you'd weigh the pros and cons of each phone against your personal needs and budget, to make the best choice. This is critical thinking in action!
scenes.image_prompt: A visual flowchart showing the steps: Question (phone icon with question mark) -> Analyze (comparison table) -> Evaluate (balance scale) -> Decision (checkmark on a selected phone).

summary: In this introductory lesson, we defined critical thinking as clear and logical thinking that helps you analyze and evaluate information. We explored its importance for both your university success and making informed decisions in everyday life. We also touched upon core components like asking questions, analyzing information, and evaluating ideas. Remember, critical thinking is a skill that gets stronger with practice!
assignment: Reflect: Think of a recent decision you made. How could you have applied critical thinking steps (question, analyze, evaluate) to make an even more informed choice?
Read: Find one short article (news, blog post, etc.) on a topic you're interested in. Identify 2-3 questions you would ask about the article's claims or sources.
Discuss: In our next session, be ready to share one example of how critical thinking could have changed an outcome in a real-life scenario.
